method: Independent source-based review; no claim of watching any of these films. Publication judgments are editorial inferences from specific treatment evidence, not ecclesiastical certification.

films.title: Un Dios prohibido
films.decision: PUBLISH: detailed reviews identify Eucharistic devotion, fidelity to religious vows and forgiveness of persecutors as the dramatic centre; the surviving prisoner testimony corroborates that moral orientation. Technical limitations and divided critical judgments about idealization are disclosed. This is an editorial recommendation of the film, not approval of a political side in the entire civil war.
films.summary: The imprisoned Claretians of Barbastro face death with a faith sustained by the Eucharist and expressed in forgiveness.
films.synopsis: In the opening months of the Spanish Civil War, a community of Claretian priests, brothers and seminarians is held captive in Barbastro. Pressure to abandon religious life, uncertainty and approaching executions test their fidelity. The story follows their preparation for death and places their ordeal alongside other Catholic victims in the city.
films.inclusion: The positive case is specifically sacramental and moral: Jerónimo José Martín’s review identifies love of the Eucharist and pardon of the killers as the film’s governing concerns. Esther Rodríguez likewise finds the faith behind their acceptance of martyrdom convincingly conveyed. On that evidence, the Library recommends this sober account of religious fidelity, while acknowledging uneven filmmaking and the dangers of idealized historical portraiture.
themes: Eucharistic devotion sustains religious vocation under coercion.
Forgiveness refuses to turn the memory of martyrdom into a demand for revenge.
films.history: The Claretian formation archive reproduces farewell testimony from the prisoners affirming forgiveness and their attachment to the Church and congregation. That record supports the central spiritual outlook; it does not authenticate every line of screenplay or every encounter.
films.liberties: A historical drama cannot reproduce an entire prison community in full. Contraste criticizes the limited individuality given to the Claretians. Beatriz Martínez’s dissenting SensaCine review argues that the film idealizes the prisoners and uses conventional persecutor characters, including an attraction between a militiwoman and a priest. These differing judgments should remain visible; its depiction is not a comprehensive history of the Spanish Civil War.
advisories: Imprisonment, humiliation, torture and executions make this a demanding martyrdom drama.
A romantic approach to a priest is rejected; parents should assess the persecution and temptation material for individual children.

films.title: The War of the Vendée
films.decision: PUBLISH: an independent contemporary viewing review identifies a positive presentation of Mass, Catholic fidelity and sacrifice; the director’s detailed interview supplies specific adaptation admissions rather than a blanket accuracy claim. Recommended as an accessible youth-performed historical drama with prominent qualifications about composite history and contested interpretation.
films.summary: A young cast dramatizes the Catholic resistance in revolutionary western France, with courage and worship at its heart.
films.synopsis: The people of the Vendée confront revolutionary pressure on their religion and rally to defend their priests and communities. Jim Morlino tells the conflict as an adventure of loyalty and sacrifice through a large cast of young performers. Battles and bereavement interrupt its moments of humour, and Catholic worship remains integral to the people’s shared life.
films.inclusion: Fr. John Zuhlsdorf’s contemporary viewing review describes the film’s presentation of Mass and its serious concern with Catholic identity, fidelity and virtue. This supports inclusion beyond the mere presence of Catholic protagonists. The Library recommends it for those willing to accept its youthful performances and modest production, accompanied by historical discussion. The recommendation neither canonizes every combatant nor justifies every action of either army.
themes: Religious worship, loyalty and costly resistance to persecution.
Courage and sacrifice require moral restraint, including toward prisoners.
films.history: The uprising belongs to the revolutionary conflicts of 1793 and the following years. Françoise Huchet’s historical study locates the opening insurrection in Maine-et-Loire in March 1793. Readers should not adopt the abbreviated chronology in publicity as a full account of the war.
films.liberties: Morlino explicitly acknowledges combining people and events and placing historical figures together who did not meet. His Catholic Answers interview names Reynald Secher among the sources and acknowledges controversy over applying the term genocide. The film is a selective dramatic retelling, not a settled adjudication of casualty totals or every disputed historical claim. Those totals are deliberately not repeated here.
advisories: Battle violence, persecution and deaths, even though performed by a young cast.
An introductory family discussion should distinguish defense of the Faith from indiscriminate revenge and historical representation from documentary evidence.
Uneven amateur acting and unusually young performers in adult roles are part of the production.

films.title: Quo Vadis
films.decision: HOLD after substantive review: the sources establish an attractive portrayal of apostolic witness and Christian charity, but also a sympathetically staged joint suicide and a romance built initially on coercion. The Library’s strict treatment-of-sin criterion requires closer assessment of the dramatic framing before a recommendation; fame and pre-1965 date do not resolve that issue. No direct viewing is claimed.
films.history: The 1951 film adapts a fictional historical romance and combines historical figures, apostolic tradition and invented characters. AFI’s page contains a visibly erroneous Nero reign date, so it cannot be copied indiscriminately. The Quo vadis encounter is a later Petrine tradition, not an episode narrated in the canonical Gospels.
films.liberties: Liz Gloyn identifies redistribution of ancient anecdotes and suicide motifs among characters. Her review also praises Christian charity and martyrdom, while questioning the romantic suggestion that a woman’s love can reform a coercive man. The issue requiring further review is framing, not mere depiction of sin.
advisories: Executions, crucifixion, people burned alive, deaths involving animals, joint suicide, coercive romantic pursuit, revealing costumes and drinking are reported.

resolutionNotes.un-dios-prohibido: Promoted with five distinct sources. Runtime omitted because Contraste90 conflicts with Aceprensa133; language crosschecked metadata. Religious rather than comprehensive political recommendation.
resolutionNotes.the-war-of-the-vendee: Promoted with explicit adaptation and historiography cautions; add18thcentury period facet. Direct Navis site inaccessible. An EDAP history PDF search result returned404 on open and was not used. No blanket family suitability or casualty figures asserted.
resolutionNotes.quo-vadis: Kept HOLD with concrete content concerns and identified next review question. Do not publish the HOLD record. AFI source metadata is stronger than Dove’s incorrect director field; neither criticism nor pious subject alone establishes incompatibility.
